subsubtopic: RIGHTS OF JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my concern that something must be done to recognize formally the injustice suffered by Canadians of Japanese origin during World War II. I do it in the context of a Government which, over its current term, has made historic and exceptional moves to guarantee human rights and fight prejudice. We have the inclusion in our new Charter of Rights of fundamental laws basic to a nation like our own, built upon diversity. The Charter forbids discrimination on the basis of race, national, or ethnic origin.
This Government has for the first time added social responsibility and equity to its primary policy objectives in multicul-turalism. It has established a race relations unit. It has added millions of dollars for new programs to fight racism. It has, with opposition Party concurrence, sponsored the first ever Canadian parliamentary inquiry into the problems faced by our visible minorities.
Having served as Minister of Multiculturalism when these and other first time initiatives on racial equity took place, I think it will be most regrettable if the Cabinet does not formally recognize the appalling consequences, fear, and hysteria brought to thousands of good and committed Canadians. It is not only for the sake of a single community, but by focusing on a tragedy and injustice of major proportions we can indicate to all that we can redress the wrongs of earlier times, especially when many of those who suffered are still here today, living with their nightmarish memories. A formal admission; the public dedication of some lasting symbol is surely the least we can provide. Otherwise a living shadow lies across the path of hope this Government has set.

subsubtopic: SUPPORT FOR FOOTWEAR IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 19, 1983, the Canadian footwear industry, because of high import penetration, rightly asked for the extension of global quotas for five years so as to permit the industry to obtain 50 per cent of the domestic market. The Canadian footwear industry is still waiting for a reply from the Government. In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, because no decision has yet been taken, many more jobs that could have been created have not materialized.
Footwear imports do not benefit the consumer. Imported shoes may cost less to make than an equivalent domestic product, but when one examines the situation as I have, they sell for the same price on the retail market.
Imports, Mr. Speaker, mean fewer jobs for Canadians. For every 2,500 pair of shoes imported, one Canadian job is lost. Last year 56 million pairs of shoes were imported into Canada, which means that Canada has exported 22,000 jobs.
Does it make sense, Mr. Speaker, to export thousands of permanent footwear industry jobs to countries such as Brazil, Korea, Taiwan, and others, which do not even allow imports of Canadian shoes?
Therefore, I call upon the Government to do everything possible, and to do the right thing regarding the Canadian footwear industry, by agreeing to its request for the extension of global quotas so that thousands of additional badly needed jobs can be created as soon as possible.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT AID SAWMILL INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are all aware of the existing conditions in the sawmill industry in Canada. The production capacity is increasing more quickly than the marketing opportunities.
Considering that many companies are now applying for federal grants in order to modernize or build plants, the Government must review those applications very carefully so as not to favour some at the expense of others.
However, care should also be taken not to lapse into an excessive and short-sighted protectionism, systematically sup-

April 11, 1984
pressing within that industry a healthy competition which exists in other areas.
There is in my riding, Mr. Speaker, a remote village with almost no means of livelihood. The people there have decided to take charge, invest a good share of their welfare allowances and join forces with a responsible partner.
The decision of the Department of Regional Economic Development is a long time coming. I hope that the Government will consider that request not on the basis of the interests of cigar-smoking fat cats who haunt the boardrooms of giant multinationals, but on the basis of rationale and equity for people who will not let themselves go to pot and be eaten away by social welfare.

subsubtopic: INPUT COSTS OF FARMERS-CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's food producers are travelling down the road toward dire straits. Farm bankruptcies have increased by 290 per cent in the past five years. Net farm income as a ratio of gross income has declined continuously from 1965. Farm operating expenses have increased 115 per cent between 1976 and 1982. They are projected to increase another 110 per cent by 1986, while farm commodity prices decline.
It is against that background that the federal Government refuses to pay farmers nearly $1 billion of their own money in the Western Grain Stabilization Fund. It is in light of these devastating economic facts that Governments have caused farm fuels to be taxed 75 per cent more than production costs. It is against these hard economic realities that the federal Government has now increased the long-term interest rates of the Farm Credit Corporation to a devastating 15 per cent. Farmers everywhere know the impact of these facts.
Today I appeal to urban Canada to rise up in anger against the federal Government. Your food security is threatened, and you are dangerously close to losing your world price advantage on low-cost foods. All Canadians must hear the message. The business of food production is seriously threatened.

subsubtopic: ATTITUDE OF QUEBEC MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to call the attention of the House to a situation concerning the fisheries on Quebec's Middle and Lower North Shore. Last
year, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans announced that the federal government would invest $30 million in that area, and now the whole operation has stopped because the Quebec Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food is preventing fishermen's committees from acquiring a site near the wharves where they could build processing plants or install an ice-house.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that it is important for the Quebec Minister to trust the fishermen from Middle and Lower North Shore, more specifically that part of the mainland between Kegaska and Blanc-Sablon facing Anticosti Island as far as Newfoundland in view of the forthcoming fishing season. Mr. Speaker, the Quebec Minister of Fisheries can certainly wait, but the fishing season will not, and the Canadian Saltfish Corporation would like to make sure that fishing facilities are available before entering into contract agreements with the various fishermen's associations of the Middle and Lower North Shore.
I therefore urge the Quebec minister without further delay to meet the requirements of the Middle and Lower North Shore fishermen.

subsubtopic: U.S.S.R.-PLIGHT OF ANDREI SAKHAROV
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Andrei Sakharov is a prominent Soviet physicist and well-known human rights activist who for years has been a respected critic of the violation of human rights in his native country, and has criticized the Soviet Union in respect of its stand on foreign relations and the immigration of some of its people. For this role Mr. Sakharov has been punished severely by the Soviet Government. He is now forced to live under constant surveillance in a remote and isolated area of the Soviet Union. He has been repeatedly refused permission to travel, and permission to receive hospital treatment for heart and kidney diseases.
Mr. Sakharov's wife, Elena Bonner, is currently in a state of badly deteriorating health and requires medical treatment for an eye ailment which is not available to her in the Soviet Union. Up to this point she has also been refused permission to travel outside the Soviet Union to receive treatment for her ailments.
Given Mr. Sakharov's stature as a crusader for the expansion of human rights in the Soviet Union, and the serious condition in which he and his wife find themselves as a direct result of their beliefs, I urge the Canadian Government to make an appeal on behalf of the Sakharovs to the Soviet Government asking that humanity be shown, that Mrs. Bonner be permitted to seek medical attention outside the Soviet Union, and that Mr. Sakharov be permitted hospital treatment. Also I would like to ask other Hon. Members of the
April 11, 1984

House concerned with and supportive of the brave campaign the Sakharovs have waged, to appeal to the Soviet Government to show some compassion in this case.

subsubtopic: ETHNIC COMMUNITIES URGED TO SUPPORT BILINGUALISM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because of my ethnic background multiculturalism has been one of my top priorities for the last 15 years as an elected provincial and federal Member. During those 15 years multiculturalism has gained considerable provincial and federal prominence, with inclusion in the new Canadian Constitution. Permit me to state again in this Assembly what I said in my constitutional speech on March 10, 1981. I said:
The extension of duality promotes and enhances our diversity. Oneness would accelerate homogenization and rapidly destroy our diversity, as it has with our neighbour to the South. The melting pot process would prevail with oneness. Multiculturalism lives because duality is alive. It is duality which promotes and enhances our diversity. Bilingualism kindles the desire for, and extension of, multiculturalism. It is the very essence of bilingualism and multiculturalism which provides diversity and gives us an exciting national fabric which makes for a new nationhood, even though some ferment must be endured.
All ethnic Canadians, and particularly those in Manitoba, should weigh seriously their support for duality and multiculturalism and their inter-relationship.

speechtext:

He will remember that during the long debate in connection with amending the Crowsnest Pass agreements he argued repeatedly that passage of the bill would lead to the employment of \ hundreds and thousands of more workers by the railways and associated companies. In the last couple of weeks CPR has reassigned work in Montreal, Toronto, and Winnipeg, so that at least 57 workers in the diesel shop, wheel shop, and powerhouse have been given their lay-off notices in the last couple of days, and at least 16 workers in the car shop have been given their lay-off notices.
Would the Minister explain to Members of the House and to the laid-off railway workers why the CPR is laying off workers, when the railway and the Minister promised so many times that we would have a greatly expanded workforce rather than less people working?

subtopic: ISSUANCE OF LAY-OFF NOTICES TO WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to point out to the Hon. Member that what we talked about in terms of a major economic expansion is indeed taking place. The railways have committed, in 1984 alone, over $1.4 billion of new purchases and expenditures. This spring we will be initiating perhaps the largest single public works project in North America when the tenders are finally awarded for the Beaver Tunnel.
In Manitoba alone there is the application of a new $14 million diesel shop, the development of a new telecommunications system, and there is double tracking taking place on some 750 kilometres of track. In other words, I could spend all afternoon talking about the number of initiatives and projects that have been launched as a result of the act that the railways are now trying to improve substantially their capacity for moving the natural resources of western Canada. What we stated in the House is in fact coming true.

subtopic: ISSUANCE OF LAY-OFF NOTICES TO WORKERS
speechtext:
I would have thought that the Minister, who has a reputation of being progressive, would agree with me and other reasonable people that a large profitable corporation like
the CPR could keep people working with very small effort because they will be expanding their facilities greatly in the next few months.

Both the CPR and
CNR have, in recent years, been contracting out more work because they say it is more efficient. Mr. Speaker, it so happens that I will be meeting with the representatives of CP Rail this afternoon to talk about a number of matters related to the operation of the grain expansion program. I will ask the questions that the Hon. Member has presented.
I want to point out that it is important to recognize that one of the objectives under the new Bill is to improve the efficiency and productivity of our transportation system to allow us to ship our grain to markets at a lower cost so that we can stay internationally competitive. We will be in a very tough competitive world of which transportation is a major component.
In terms of the adjustments that companies must make between workers, we have spoken to them about making sure that those adjustments are made in a tolerant and proper way. I do not think that the Hon. Member would want us in any way to impede the ability of the railways to provide a more productive system, because that would then rebound upon the ability of grain farmers in western Canada to sell their products.

subsubtopic: REVENUE COLLECTED FROM CAPITAL GAINS TAX
speechtext:
There is no capital gains tax per se. Rather, under the personal income tax system one-half of total capital gains or losses are included in the calculation of income for taxation at normal personal tax rates. Effective October 1, 1983, the tax on the inflationary portion of capital gains earned on moneys invested in an Indexed Security Investment Plan (ISIP) was eliminated. Under the corporate tax system one-half of the excess of capital gains over losses accrued since 1971 and realized on the
disposition of certain properties is included in income and taxed at normal tax rates. Although accurate data on both total personal and total corporate income tax revenues are available, the portion directly attributable to net capital gains can only be estimated. On the basis of the latest available published information for the 1981 taxation year, total federal and provincial revenues from the taxation of capital gains are estimated to be $1.6 billion.

ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-INTEREST RATES FOR FARM CREDIT Mr. Vic Althouse (Humboldt-Lake Centre) moved:
That this House condemns the Government for abandoning farmers who are having problems with credit costs and falling commodity prices as demonstrated
(1)	by the higher interest rates and shortened terms imposed on Farm Credit Corporation loans;
(2)	by the Government's lack of support for the agribond concept thereby denying farmers access to funds at lower costs; and
(3)	by the failure of the Government to renew the 4 per cent interest rebate program offered by the Farm Credit Corporation to farmers in Financial distress.
He said: Mr. Speaker, what we have before us today is a problem that is approaching crisis conditions for farmers across Canada. Yesterday the Minister of Agriculture, (Mr. Whelan), who is in charge of the Farm Credit Corporation, announced new credit terms and time periods for loans under the Farm Credit Corporation. It was a real shock to farmers who were expecting some relief from interest rates and an expansion of Farm Credit Corporation to meet the needs of many farmers who now have to refinance and re-group in order to meet this year's financing requirements to seed one more crop.
Yesterday the Minister proposed to increase the interest rate in existence before Christmas of 13 per cent to a long-term rate of 15 per cent. He gave us five sets of terms, five-year, ten-year and 20-year. The five-year term is at 14 per cent. Five-year term loans of some banks can be obtained for 13.25 per cent. At some credit unions the same loans can be obtained at 12.75 per cent. The larger loans just will not be acceptable for the needs of farmers at this moment.
Moving on quickly to the second point in the overall discussion of the motion before us before I begin to explain how I believe we got to where we are, and to propose some longer-term and shorter-term solutions, if we can believe what the Minister was saying in the House, in committee and on the hustings, the Government was to bring in some some sort of agri-bond program in the Budget brought down in February. There was no agri-bond announcement then, simply an announcement to submit the idea for further study. The Budget has been down for seven or eight years and so far no committee has been struck to do that job.
The third item for which we are condemning the Government today relates to the matter of farmers who two years ago
April 11, 1984

were determined to have been in financial distress. The Minister, through FCC, initiated a special program to help farmers facing financial disaster. He proposed to rebate them 4 per cent of the cost of their loans, bringing down most of their loans to 12.75 per cent, close to 13 per cent. That program has run out. Several thousand farmers in that category now face bankruptcy and there has been no action on the part of the Government to deal with that problem.
1 want to take a few moments to go back over the record of farm financing. As a sideline, we will be looking at the record of this Government and this Minister because that is one of the recurring themes throughout the period I will be covering. I want to give some idea of the numbers involved in farm credit and farm financing. I have chosen the years 1971 and 1981 so that we can get a handle on the changes that have occurred in agriculture over that time period. I regret that I cannot use numbers more current than 1981, but they are the latest numbers that we are able to get that are not just estimates.
Let us go back to 1971 and look at the amount of credit outstanding at that time. I have here a market commentary on the cost of farm inputs and finance put out by Agriculture Canada in 1983. The most up to date figures there show that in 1971 the total credit extended was $4.6 billion. By 1981, the amount of farm credit outstanding to farmers was $18.4 billion, an increase of just over four times within that decade. When you look at farm incomes within that period, there are some very revealing figures. Most people familiar with agriculture know that 1971 was a disastrous year for most commodities produced in Canada. Farmers had suffered a series of poor markets and net incomes were extremely low at that time. They got back to normal in 1974. For the first time in some years, net farm income in Canada was at $3.5 billion.
According to the estimates produced by Agriculture Canada at the Outlook Conference, ten years later, 1984 would show a net farm income in the neighbourhood of $3.5 billion. A decade has passed and net farm incomes stuck at that level. In between there were a couple of blips when it went to almost $4 billion and a few times when it dropped below $3.5 billion, down to $3.2 billion. Incomes have been extremely stable for Canadian farmers, but what would the dollar buy in that same period? There was a deterioration in the buying power of the Canadian agricultural dollar in that period of time. The 1974 dollar would buy almost two and one-half times as much as the 1984 dollar.
In real terms, farm incomes have been more than cut in half. No small wonder farmers have turned to the only source of funds they can find, debt. That is why the debt load increased four times from 1971 to 1981. If we had more up to date statistics, I am sure they would show that the debt load would have increased almost that much again between 1981 and the current year.
The effects on the farming community are fairly clearcut. I simply refer to some of the problems that the extra debt and the increase in interest rates have brought about. I refer to a recent brief sent to most Members of this House by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. They say that in 1971,
Supply
17.9 per cent of Farm Credit Corporation repayments due were in arrears. It will be recalled that 1971 ranks as one of the poorest years for Canadian farmers, almost ranking with the 1931-32 period.
What do we find in 1983? The repayments due to Farm Credit Corporation were 17.5 per cent, almost the same. There is a striking parallel between the poorest year in living memory and our recent experience.
There were a couple of interesting differences between 1971 and 1981 that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture was quick to point out. These should be on the record to show that to some extent the current crop of farmers are worse off than those who suffered through the 1971 period. The percentage of interest costs on returns to capital in self-employed and unpaid family labour in 1971 was 18 per cent. In 1982 that percentage had doubled to 36 per cent. Another way of expressing it is that a 3 per cent on total farmers' equity in 1971 represented 52 per cent of his net income. In other words, for half of his income he was living on his investment equity.
In 1982, the return on the farmer's investment equity represented 91 per cent of his net income. This means that that poor man earned very little after paying for labour, management and so on. He is simply living off of the equity he has in his farm.
Another way to put it is that of total farm capital, the interest bill in 1971 would have eaten up 82 per cent of the returns to capital in self-employed and unpaid family labour. What really hurts is that by 1982, that figure rose to 140 per cent of the farmer's income. That amount went to paid and unpaid family labour. It is small wonder that farmers are going broke. Operations are costing them 50 cents for every dollar of net income they once earned.
A heavy burden has been placed on Canadian farmers. This burden shows up when looking at the bankruptcy statistics. Raw data is available, but if we call the 1979 bankruptcy index 100-and there were many bankruptcies in 1979-in 1984, the same index would be 620. In a mere five years, farm bankruptcies have increased by 6.2 times.
We can dig those numbers out of the statistics but statistics are slow to respond to current affairs. Statistics are always two or three years behind the times as you know, Mr. Speaker. By looking at the statistics we can see the problems that have developed. But we do not need those statistics to illustrate what we see when we go to the farming communities. We only need look around the farming communities to see that farmers are in trouble, particularly the younger farmers who have started up in the last 10 or 12 years and those farmers who have expanded in an attempt to include the next generation.
This effect can be seen even in western Canada where the agricultural recession did not hit as hard. When land was for sale in the past, it was taken off the listings within a week or two. However, most of the small newspapers in my riding have advertised lands for sale throughout the winter. Apparently, those lands will still be for sale in the spring. People are not

April 11, 1984
Supply
interested in buying land from farmers who want to unload their farms. People who are facing debts greater than they think they can manage are attempting to sell out but cannot find buyers.
What has the Minister's response been to that need? The interest rates have risen. When I and other members of my caucus tour the farming communities, we meet far more farmers who are complaining of credit problems than we did in previous years. We hear from fertilizer and fuel dealers who, last year, extended credit to farmers and have not yet collected the money owed them. Those dealers must make a decision, as must the farmers, about going on for another year.
We sometimes hear of fairly large farm operators who are no longer dealing for their fuel and fertilizer needs with their local community dealers because their credit is no longer good. They are shopping further afield with the hope that the size of their business needs will attract a supplier from communities 30, 40 or 50 miles away. In that way they can receive credit for one more year, with the hope that the prices of grain or livestock will rise so they will be able to pay their debts.
A crisis is occurring and government Members have not addressed that particular set of problems. Increasing the interest rate does not meet the needs of farmers. The whole attitude to the Farm Credit Corporation seems to have changed over the last decade. The Farm Credit Corporation was once the means of providing long-term credit to agriculture so that land could change hands from one generation to another. At the urging of the Minister responsible, the FCC has deliberately pulled itself back from that long-term market to make room for the banks. That was stated policy during the debate on the Bank Act. What the Government had in mind was even urged by the Official Opposition.
The only role that seems to be left open to the FCC is that of a financer of last resort. When all else fails, when private banking institutions will not provide any more funds to a farmer, he goes to the Farm Credit Corporation to try to consolidate his debts and get a longer term on his loan with a fixed rate of interest. The Minister, by increasing the interest rates of the FCC, has effectively taken away that option. The only option left for a great many of these farmers now is nothing short of going bankrupt or, in many cases, attempting unsuccessfully to sell their assets and try to find some other form of livelihood.
We know that the basic problem is one of farm income. We know that there has been no general recognition of longer-term programs that would keep farmers from getting into this mess. We know that there has been very little attention paid to improving the market so that farmers can recover a larger proportion of their costs from the marketplace. We know that there are no stabilization programs to respond quickly when incomes drop. We know that these things must be addressed in the House. However, we know that the solutions to those problems are medium and long-term solutions and, as John Maynard Keynes was fond of saying in the 1930s, in the long run, we are all dead. That, Mr. Speaker, will happen to several thousand operators in the country because of the inability of
this Government and the previous Government to create a long-term and a medium-term policy.
We are left with only one source of hope for these people, and that is an immediate short-term policy to provide adequate amounts of farm credit, guaranteed prices and interest rates that are low enough to allow a farmer to get out of the mess in which he has found himself. However, this will not happen as long as the current attitude persists.
We in the NDP have presented an outline for an agri-bond program. We proposed that that would be a way of maintaining an increasing amount of money within the agricultural sector. We think that agriculture is still a growth sector which can provide a great deal of spin-off growth to the rest of the economy. We are concerned about the fact that the official agriculture spokesman for the Conservative Party, the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer), has been quite vocal in the press and has said that he does not think the agri-bond system will work. He has been quoted as saying that it may do more harm than good, particularly given the impact of such a program on land values. I regret that that is the attitude which has been taken. I hope that is not the reason the committee on agri-bonds has been delayed. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that this House-

speechtext: For debate, the Hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan).

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make one comment about The Manitoba Co-Operator. I am written about at length at times in that magazine. I do not think I have ever been contacted by the reporter either. Some of the things he says are very inaccurate. Sometimes we do write letters to The Manitoba Co-Operator correcting them. I find it difficult to be criticised by a paper that maintains it is a supporter of farmers when some of the criticism is so unfair.
I would like to make it very clear that we all realize that we cannot finance people out of economic problems. There seems to be an idea that you can finance them out of their difficulty by lending them more money. In many instances the reason they are in difficulty is because of the way money was lent to them in the first place by other lending institutions. The Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) neglected to point out that if you check the financial statements of some of the farmers who are in arrears you will find they have been in economic trouble for as many as seven or eight years. Some of them have not been able to make payments on their loans for four years. Then these operations are put up for sale.
What can we do with farms in that position? Let us look at what we did last year. The Farm Credit Corporation loaned $750 million to people in Canada. Around 60 per cent of that went to the banks to refinance these people. Before last year I believe 18 per cent was the most that went to other lending institutions. We gave the banks approximately $500 million that they could have lent back to the agricultural community, but they did not.
Let us remember that the farmers have some say about what they get for their products. The poultry farmers produce
Supply
broilers, eggs and turkeys. The dairy farmers produce industrial dairy products and fluid milk. The farmers in some provinces contract their crops for food processing. In the Province of Ontario there have been marketing boards for those commodities for 40 years. The day they sign the contract they know what they are going to receive for about 30 different commodities if they deliver a high quality product. In that agreement you get crop insurance and other things which are taken out of the contract. They do not have to advance any money at that time for those things. We must consider what these people do to help themselves.
I am going to try to be as quick as I can, Mr. Speaker. I am delighted to respond to the Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre. This gives me a chance to review the actions the Government has taken to help farmers and the Canadian agri-food industry in short term as well as in building a solid foundation for the future. I would like to make it clear to the Members that there are a lot of farmers in financial difficulty.
I understand that. The figures show this. However, percentage-wise they are in less difficulty than small and big business in Canada. That means that in total they are probably a little bit better off.
Last year net farm income dropped by 2 percentage points after suffering a 9 per cent drop in 1982. This year we are hoping for an increase in net farm income of 5 per cent or 6 per cent. Even with that improvement we will continue to have about 5 per cent of Canadian farmers in serious financial difficulty and another 5 per cent to 10 per cent in some degree of difficulty. Some of the farmers will not make it. No Minister of Agriculture and no politician can guarantee that every farmer will stay in business. We cannot do that for any business person in Canada.
However, what I and the Government can and have done is to provide farmers with safety nets to cushion the falls in production and market prices and to help cope with the most severe aspects of the cost-price squeeze through emergency financial assistance programs. We have also provided ladders to help farmers improve their incomes through research and development programs, market assistance and so on. In total my Department will spend more than $1.2 billion this year.
I have a breakdown by province of my Department's expenditures. I ask the permission of the House to table these with my comments as I will not go over them at this time. These figures do not include the spending in the national capital area which benefits the agri-food industry across the great country of Canada.
As I said, the spending of my Department will amount to about $1.2 billion this year. Other federal departments also contribute to strengthening Canadian agriculture. Transport Canada spends about $700 million. When you add this all up, the federal Government is spending about $2.1 billion a year on agriculture. In addition, in the last fiscal year the provinces spent about $1.2 billion on agriculture. That is a grand total of about $3.3 billion between the two levels of government. That does not include the lending of money by the Farm Credit

April 11, 1984
Supply
Corporation which amounted to $750 million last year and will rise to as much as $825 million this year.
In short, Mr. Speaker, we are talking about a very substantial contribution to Canadian agriculture. For the Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre to suggest we have abandoned the farmers is absurd. Let us look at some of the special programs we have initiated to help hard-pressed farmers in recent years.
In the June 1982 Budget we provided $200 million for the Farm Credit Corporation to administer a special lending program at rates 4 per cent below the prevailing rate.
I see some people from the CFA sitting in the gallery.
It is interesting how rapidly the requests change from $200 million to $1 billion, this type of thing. The requests are not very consistent in what they ask for, either. Flowever, we did provide what we said we would. We provided $200 million extra.
The April, 1983 Budget provided a further $100 million in funds for that same special program, providing a special lending program of rates four point below the prevailing rate. Previous to this, Mr. Speaker, in 1981, the Budget provided for $45 million for debt refinancing by farmers with an interest rate of 5 percentage points for the first two years of the loan.
A lot of farmers use the small business bond with the special interest rate, which was approximately half of the current rate of interest at that time, providing low interest loans to qualifying farmers. I know a lot of people are aware of what that amounted to and what it did.
The Farm Credit Corporation in April 1982-1983 provided $145 million, I repeat, from its regular funds at a special reduced rate of interest. I am sure Hon. Members know that even though a lot of people received that reduced interest rate, it all depended on what production entity they were in. If they were producing for this open and free market system, which so many people talk about, hogs and beef or potatoes, and refused to get into any other crop and some kind of a marketing system where they have some say in the market, but depended on everyone else to look after them, they were the ones in the most financial difficulty.
The other farmers I mentioned, Mr. Speaker, who had some say in the marketplace, they are not the ones going broke. They are not the ones who are applying for the big loans either, because they can go to the banks and other lending institutions and get loans right away. Even if they only have a low equity in their operation, they know in time they can pay that off, whereas if you go with high equity into one of these other production entities like potatoes, red meat, pork or beef, there are statistics which show it disappears, because the sick marketplace is not giving you a return. The market is not being fair with you at all.
Further to the accusation that we have not done anything, the most recent Budget in February contained several items of benefit to the farming community, including the generous treatment of capital gains for retiring farmers. That is why we
have again done some checking on farms which are advertised for sale, because these farmers will be able to have $250,000 tax free, if they are selling. A lot of them are waiting for that change in the legislation.
Further to the accusation that the Government has abandoned farmers, let us look at some of the regular programs of my Department, and some of our new initiatives. I mentioned that my Department is now spending just over $1.2 billion a year. I will give you a breakdown by major activity. Our research department is spending $237 million in the current fiscal year. You read so much lately about how we are cutting back on research. That is up by $35 million from the previous year. I would say it is significantly up. Our research program represents well over half of the agri-food research done in Canada. The private sector should be doing much more than it is. But some people in the private sector and in the other Parties, especially the Conservative Party, keep saying we should spend more public funds on research. I agree, but 1 hope they are saying the same thing to the food processing industry, the grocery products manufacturers, and so on, who do not even spend . 1 per cent of their gross national product on research.
I should mention that our capital improvement program for the research branch over the coming ten years is close to $500 million. There is a false impression that we have reduced our spending on research. I hope these figures have cleared that up.
Our regional development program, which includes things like record of performance testing, as well as the sub-agreements and development programs we have in provinces and regions, amounts to about $55 million per year.
We have changed the Farm Credit Corporation to make it more realistic. For instance, the Chairman of the Farm Credit Corporation was a grain and beef farmer in Saskatchewan before he came here. Real Lambert from Quebec is a dairy farmer. Claude Palmer from Prince Edward Island is a potato farmer. Irene Perlich from Alberta has a cow-calf operation and an auction mart. She knows agriculture. From Ontario we have a former bank manager of the Imperial Bank of Commerce. Doctor Trant is from the Stabilization Board and Paul Babey is from Alberta. So you can see, Mr. Speaker, that the Farm Credit Corporation represents people from all over Canada. It can be identified as truly an organization which understands Canadian farmers. These people will have a much better understanding of what is going on.
We are spending $215 million this year on regulation and inspection. This service is to help maintain quality and hence the premium attached to Canadian agri-food products.
Let us look at some of the safety nets provided by my Department's Farm Income Services Branch. We have been spending an average of about $350 million a year on stabilization payments for named and designated commodities in recent years. I was pleased to announce, as I am sure all Hon. Members are aware, the agreement we have reached in triparty legislation for a new red meat stabilization plan. This should not only provide an improved level of support for
April 11, 1984

participating farmers but also help to reduce the disparities which exist between provinces. We offered them an even better program in 1977 and they turned it down. Even farm organizations turned it down, saying it would be too rich and would cause all kinds of problems. Some of them have short memories.
With respect to the Western Grain Stabilization Plan, like the red meat program, the Speech from the Throne mentioned that the Western Grain Stabilization Plan would be improved, and I hope we will be able to make an announcement in that regard in the very near future. Coming up with a new formula has not been an easy task because, despite the individual problems that many western farmers are experiencing, their overall grain receipts last year, $6.15 billion, was second only to the record set in 1981 of $6.2 billion. Commodity prices were lower and costs were higher, but the sheer volume of sales, 36.7 million metric tonnes of grain kept the overall net income figure above the trigger level. So there was no payment.
A few other figures help to put the western grain stabilization issue into perspective. Since the program began in 1976, farmers have contributed just under $350 million to it. The federal Government contributed nearly $700 million and it has paid $204 million in interest on the funds. Last year alone the Government paid about $130 million into the fund. The total producer and government payments into the fund amount ot $1.25 billion, and when you subtract the pay-outs of $368 million, you are left with the current fund balance of $885 million. That is where it stood at the end of 1983. We are talking about a lot of money, Mr. Speaker.
With respect to crop insurance, let us not forget that the federal Government is contributing around $150 million a year towards this excellent co-operative program. We pay 50 per cent of the premiums, the producers pay the other 50 per cent, and the provinces administer the program, and if it is any good they try to take 95 per cent of the credit for it. Saskatchewan thought it was so good that it appointed a minister just to be in charge of crop insurance, looking after the producers' money and the money which the federal Government contributes to that plan, amounting to about $56 million a year. For instance, when you add up the interest free advance payments, and all of these other things, it amounts to nearly $900 million for the three prairie provinces.
Taking Saskatchewan alone, with interest free advance payments, both under the Wheat Board and the other program we have, and the money put into the Farm Credit Corporation, the actual expenditure on agriculture in Saskatchewan is nearly $500 million in one year. The Province of Saskatchewan, knowing full well its main industry is agriculture, spends about $86 million on agriculture. Last year our actual expenditure was some $130 million. That is one of the greatest provinces for agriculture production. But, again, the province shows that it does not think agriculture is so important, and I can show you in other provinces, Mr. Speaker, that things are the same.

We also guarantee farm improvement loans; more than $200 million a year under the program so that farmers can buy equipment. But, $500 million interest free, that is nothing; that is what the Members say. Well, those are programs we put into effect for all crops, not just those under the Canadian Wheat Board.
The Crowsnest Pass freight rates have been talked about, Mr. Speaker. They have an effect on farm income, especially prairie farm income, as everyone knows. Everyone talks about the rise in the cost of shipping grain, but few people mention that under the Western Grain Stabilization Act there have been reductions of about 75 per cent in the cost of shipping canola oil and meal, linseed oil and meal, sunflower seeds and oil, mustard see, triticale, dehydrated alfalfa and special crops. The rate has gone from a high of over $42 a ton to the current low of $7 or $8 per ton to ship that product to ports of export. But you never hear about that; all you hear about is the increase in costs. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mul-roney) spoke today about this tremendous increase in costs. Well, the farmers producing those products will save about $34 a ton if it is passed on to them by the trade.
Another thing that I do not hear the Government getting much credit for is providing credit needed to sell grain on today's world market. You would think the Government was not even involved in that. The Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), who was the Minister of Agriculture in a previous Government, knows. He had to sit and listen to how the Government had to guarantee the sales. That amounts to billions of dollars, and some of those sales are pretty risky. But if the Government did not do that those sales would not be made.
The Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Alt-house) seems to think that we are oblivious to what is going on around us and in other countries. We cannot do that and we know it. They were attacking the Farm Credit Corporation interest rates. Well, they must not forget that no other lending institution is giving the same long-term rates, regardless of what the Members say. We have done a study on this and I challenge the Hon. Member to find the kind of long-term interest rates we provide in any other lending institution.
We know farmers are backing off from buying. We are still working very hard on the agri-bond sector and some of the other things which are so important. But I repeat: You cannot finance all the farmers out of the economic problems they are in.

I cancelled the meetings so I would have a chance to be here to listen to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) respond to the motion before us today. In view of the very serious economic conditions many Canadian farmers are facing, I was certain that he

would utilize this opportunity to make some policy announcements and provide encouragement, to the effect that some additional dollars had been found to help those farmers who are locked into loans with interest rates in the neighbourhood of 16.75 per cent, and indeed those who qualify for the 4 per cent interest rate program.
The Minister has been telling us and the industry over the last six or eight months that he was about to announce some special program. We have seen some press reports recently that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has provided the Minister with the authority, I believe it was under Bill C-88, to borrow an additional $75 million. I believe there is a special fund in the neighbourhood of $275 million this year as compared to $200 million last year.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member knows that these loans vary from 15 per cent to 16.75 per cent. We are working on a program, and I wish I was able to announce it today because we want to do even better than the announcement I made the other day concerning 14 per cent for five years as we can borrow money on the long term market at a better interest rate for five years then we can for 10 or 20. We do not know what is going to happen in the private money market, but we are also working on programs which will amortize loans to farmers.
I am sure the Hon. Member is aware that in some instances farmers have been unable to make a payment even with the reduced interest rate. If we gave some of them the money free they would not even make a good living for themselves. Some farmers are suggesting that we take over the farm. That is not much different than giving them the money free. They say, put them under an operational management plan. Then, in three to five years, if they were in a financially sound condition, they would be given an opportunity to buy the farm back from us. I am getting a lot of letters from farmers in Manitoba suggesting this very thing. They cannot make their payments, they are three or four years in arrears, and please do something to let them continue on with their family farms.
I do not know what we are going to come up with, Mr. Speaker. As I said yesterday in the House, the opposition Members concern is great, but it is no greater than mine regarding what we can do to save these people and keep them in production, because they are generally good producers. Some of them have been farming all their lives. Some are new farmers. There is every kind of farmer you can think of, every age bracket, and a lot of them are young people who have maybe over-capitalized or over-spent.
Some of the farmers say to me, when I make a speech about how we might assist them, and I am sure the other Members
hear this, do not help them because they got in that trouble themselves. In some instances this may be true, but we will need all these food producers for the future because the biggest challenge we face is food production.

Mr. Speaker, for some reason or other I sense the Minister has lost his resolve to go to bat for the farmers who are in serious difficulty. It is a crisis situation. Look at the record since his Government was returned to office. In 1979 there were some 125 farm bankruptcies recorded; in 1983 it was roughly 500. Those are the official statistics and they do not tell the whole story. In the first two months of this year farm bankruptcies were up 110 per cent in western Canada. The Minister seems to lay the blame on the managerial abilities of producers. The fact is that in most cases these producers are in trouble because of things beyond their control-high interest rates, high input costs; fuel prices have doubled under this Government's National Energy Program since 1980. All of these things put together have increased input costs by roughly 35 percent, while commodity prices are roughly at the 1972 and 1973 level.
The Minister can certainly offer more relief than simply the kind of flim-flam he gave us here today. I know that he said during the last election campaign that he did not believe that the producers of food should have an onerous tax regime on fuels used for farm production. Is he still of the same opinion? What will he do about facilitating and moving forward our motion, which has now been referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, to do away with the 9 per cent federal sales tax on fuel used for the production of food?

First, I want to say that the province the Hon. Member comes from, which is a very rich province, I believe has five loan programs for farmers. A lot of them find themselves in real great financial difficulty.
Do not talk about Alberta. You have a national responsibility. Do not weasel out of it.

It is a giant responsibility and that is why his province has been involved in these lending programs. They have made loans to a lot of people to whom, they now admit, they should not have loaned money at preferred interest rates. Those loan programs are still in effect in Alberta. Some of them are coming to us now asking the Farm Credit Corporation to take over their loans, loans from the Alberta Treasury Bank, for example. That great free enterprise province has a bank which it owns itself. I must say that it did provide some services to the farmers.
When the Member talks about the energy program, it would even be worse than it is if we did everything that the Province of Alberta wanted. It wanted world prices for oil and wanted us to pay even higher prices for the energy.

You charge world prices.
April 11, 1984

I tried to get away from the fact that it had nothing to do with energy prices. It has a lot to do with energy prices.
I agree with the Hon. Member on one point. There should not be any fuel tax on any food production entity.
What are you going to do about it?

There should not be any fuel tax on any food production entity in Canada. I still say that, and still fight for that belief. But let us not be so unfair as to say that the total increase in energy cost is our fault, because the provinces that have the energy are the ones that created the main increase in the price for farmers in Canada as far as that goes. They were demanding what the OPEC countries had said was a realistic price, that they should have the same thing.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to enter into the debate on the motion which was put forward by the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse). When I read the motion, I suspected that the Member had found on his desk a copy of the ten-point agricultural program we proposed over a year ago and decided to put a few of our points into his motion. He has finally come on side respect to our agri-bond concept. It is good to see that the New Democratic Party is finally supporting that position.
The Hon. Member says that he is concerned about agriculture. We wish he had had the same concern when we were debating the Crow legislation, that Bill of great importance to western Canada. I will talk about that issue since it has increased the cost to western Farmers this year.
Supply
Before discussing that issue, I want to deal with some of the points raised by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) a few moments ago. The most important fact about farmers, who are in a high risk business, is that they are price takers, not price setters. They require positive indicators that show the markets will be there for them, that prices will be reasonable and their input costs will not be there for them, that prices will be reasonable and their input costs will not go out of line. The indication they have received form the Government during the last year and a half is that it has given up on them. The Minister of Agriculture is incapable of getting the concurrence from the national Cabinet that will allow him to assist the farmers in distress areas across the country.
The Minister is quick to point out that farmers who are involved in supply management are not in as great distress. He is correct. The reason they are not in as much distress is that they are producing for an internal market that is controlled and, therefore, allows them to set the price. However, I remember when the Minister recently chastised the American farmers for limiting control of production on grain. Is he now suggesting to grain farmers today that they limit the production of grain in this country? Is that a solution to the desperate plight that many of those farmers find themselves in? Since the Minister recently said that this was unchristian, I wonder whether he is talking out of both sides of his mouth on this question.
The Minister talks about the Agricultural Stabilization Act. The Government must pay out $350 million under the Agricultural Stabilization Act because farm prices for those farm products are less than the five-year average. That is a horrendous fact and something about which I would not want to brag.
I happen to have the statistics that were provided by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. It shows that farmers are receiving the same realized net income this year as they were in 1971. I remember 1971 very well, because that was the year we were selling barley in western Canada at three bushels for $1. It was the most depressed time in agricultural history since the 1930s. Farmers are experiencing the same depression today, because the realized net income this year is the same as it was in 1971.
Input costs have gone through the roof. Interest rates, as the motion points out, are a huge cost to farmers, plus the fact that the prices that farmers receive for their livestock, grains and other commodities they produce are not sufficient to meet the increased costs of production. Farmers simply cannot tolerate another period of high interest rates. Presently, the average farm carries a substantially greater proportion of debt than it did 10 or 20 years ago. Today, Canadian farmers are carrying $20 billion worth of debt, so that even an increase of one per cent in interest rates would put them in a distressed position.
When interest rates went up to 22 per cent two years ago, farmers began to live on their equity. At the same time, as land prices dropped and machinery prices went down because no one was buying, their equity decreased. Many farmers are

April 11, 1984
Supply
now incapable of obtaining sufficient capital to put their crops in this year. This brings up another point. There was a time 20 years when most farmers had built up sufficient savings to be able to finance a crop from their bank accounts, in case of disaster. Today, most farmers borrow their money in order to plant their crops. If they lose a crop they are in serious trouble. Sure, we have farm insurance which should assist them, but it is generally not enough to keep them in business to give them the costs that are attached.
Farm Credit has put forward some very interesting statistics. The Minister says, and I think I quote him correctly, that ten per cent of the farmers are in financial difficulty and 5 per cent to 10 per cent are in some degree of difficulty. The statistics of the Farm Credit Corporation have just been put before the Agricultural Committee. They show that there were 86 Farm Credit foreclosures last year.
Then we have the statistics that are more revealing. The Minister says that farmers are doing better than other businesses. Farmers are experiencing less bankruptcies than both small and big businesses. But the difficult part and the reason you cannot relate the two is that many people are in and out of small and large businesses over their lifetimes. Very few businesses are family businesses that have continued for generation after generation.
In the case of agriculture that does not happen. A son generally takes over from a father who has taken over from his father. There is pride in continuing the family farm. When you push out a generation of farmers, you are not just pushing out one individual, you are pushing out a whole family that has built a farm over decades and generations. When we lose 86 people, we lose 86 people generally with a tremendous amount of farm experience.
As far as businesses are concerned, in most cases people are in and out of businesses. I know it is hard to lose a small business. Our family went through that. But it is not the same as if one were to lose the family farm. My grandfather came to this country, cut the trees, and began planting. That is part of my family. And so we hear 86 farmers are out. It does not seem like a lot but that tells a lot. Here is the more interesting statistics. Two hundred and sixty-six farmers who had a Farm Credit loans voluntarily went out of business. They did not wait until the sheriff came and seized their assets. They said with pride that they could not make it anymore. As the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) said, it was not because of their management, but because of outside forces, such as high costs of fuel, interest rates, fertilizer et cetera, together with low commodity prices. This is what put them out of business. With pride, they said, "We will shut down and get out before we lose everything". They did it voluntarily.
But here is another statistic that concerns me. As of January 1, 1984, 14,265 Farm Credit accounts were in arrears. That means farmers are having difficulty paying their bills this year. The Minister and that Government cannot get their act together to get the Western Grain Stabilization Bill passed.
They cannot get their act together to get the advanced payments legislation passed through this House. We have said we would pass both Bills quickly. They have not been able to move on Farm Credit interest rates. I remember when we went to camp we had a song we called, "announcements, announcements". This activity happened at the beginning of each day. The Minister keeps telling farmers-we get the press releases, they come shuffling through our office-that he is going to announce, as he just said, some great thing for interest rates for farmers. The Minister is going to announce something on stabilization for red meats, that the Government will soon have a Bill on western grain stabilization to assist farmers. While the Minister is saying he is going to do something for farmers, every day another one bites the dust. That announcement will not do the Minister the good of a hill of beans. It will not do him any good at all.
What farmers are looking for is an indicator that this Minister will act quickly, because they are putting crops in the ground this spring. They are having to buy new cattle for their feed lots. They are having to keep their livelihood together and they are not getting the indicators that are essential to deciding whether to continue in production and continue to fight to hang on until something happens with commodity prices. Those are serious statistics.
If you say that Farm Credit lends approximately just under half the money in Canada to farmers, it means you have to double that to get the exact figures. If you look at the number of losses the Farm Credit Corporation has had, probably the statistics show there are less arrears and less bankruptcies than the banks experience. In actuality things are probably worse than that. A serious situation exists.
What happened yesterday? What indicator did we have to the farmers that this Government was concerned about one of their chief costs, namely interest rates? We had a press release that said interest rates were going up 1 per cent; not that interest rates were going to remain stable, not an announcement that would indicate the Government is concerned about farmers.
What about this new red meat proposal the Minister has just waved in front of us? We do not even know what it is. Do we hear that the Government is ready to act on it? No, Mr. Speaker, The indicator we have is that interest rates are going up 1 per cent. What does that say to a farm community?
The Hon. Member for Bruce Grey (Mr. Gurbin) brought forward a motion which was passed in this House. It passed in this House because all Members are concerned about this problem. The Hon. Member for Vegreville brought forward a motion on farm fuels. It was passed in this House during Private Members' Hour. This was a private members motion that said that all Members in this House are concerned about farmers. Members want these motions to go to the finance committee to be dealt with because there might be something here to assist farmers. But what does the Liberal majority in the finance committee do? They said "We can't deal with this. We must have a study. We have to hire a person in the Library
April 11, 1984

of Parliament to do a study. We hope we will have it ready some time in May".
Shame.

After most farmers have put their crops in the ground, the Government might find some time to study this proposal that has been put forward. Not that the Government would act on it immediately because there is a serious problem in this country, or that we should sit day and night until we come up with a solution. No, that does not happen, Mr. Speaker. We hear that the Government does not have the time and it needs a further study.
It frustrates me as a Member representing farmers who I see selling their land, putting their land up for sale, or going bankrupt every day. Farmers are asking me what they ought to do. Other Members have put the horrendous statistics on the record about what is happening. Bankruptcies were up 300 per cent in Alberta between January and February this year over last year. There were 480 bankruptcies across Canada in 1983.
I want to talk a little bit about the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Humbolt-Lake Centre which says that farmers are in difficulty. I want to talk about what his Party suggested we do when the Crow Bill was put forward. Western farmers have serious difficulties because of interest rates, because of the costs of fertilizer sprays, seed, machinery and so forth. What is added to that this year is an increased freight bill because of the Crow legislation. The Hon. Member who put forward this motion today had a lot to say about the Crow. He is the deputy critic for transport in the New Democratic Party and he only managed to attend 68 per cent of the meetings. The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), who was the critic, managed to attend 61 of the 66 meetings. What about Members on this side? The Hon. Member for Vegreville who was heading our committee never missed one meeting. He attended all the meetings.
What about Winnipeg?
Check the record.

Members from each of the provinces who represented our Party, the main representatives from Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta all attended 63 out of 66 meetings. That showed their concern for the western farmer. We changed that Bill substantially even though it was put forward in a manner not acceptable to this Party.
The more serious situation was that the Hon. Member put forward a motion which would amend the safety net. He was very concerned about farm costs. His motion was rather lengthy and concerned the shippers' share limitation. It was similar to the original motion moved by the Minister of Transport, with which I will deal in a minute. However, it had one basic difference, that it would put the price ratio limit per calendar year at 3 per cent.

If that motion had been passed, farmers this year would have been paying more for transportation than they are under the Government's Bill. It exposed producers to a substantial increase in freight rates. Under the NDP plan, their rates could have risen to $6 per tonne before the safety net limit was reached.
The safety net in the Crow legislation is all that farmers have as protection that their freight rates will not rise above what they can afford in transportation costs. If the six-grain limit of the Government which is now in effect remains without change, it could very well prohibit the shipping of barley, oats and rye by 1990 from western Canada to ports because it would cost more than the cost of production. The Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre never addressed that. He just addressed the levels. If he was as concerned about farmers in Saskatchewan as I am about the ones in Alberta, he would know that the six-grain level has to be addressed because it is unfair to coarse grain producers. If costs continue as they are and world prices do not escalate, they will be unable to ship their grains.
The Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board made a wonderful announcement for farmers! He said that farmers in western Canada had to expect a lower initial price from the Wheat Board this year for their production. That is another indicator of which the Government is proud.
You are kidding.

No, that was the announcement. Just as farmers were prepared to put seed in the ground, the Government came forward in an attempt to prepare them for the problem and said that their initial prices this year will be less than they were last year. These are the indicators which the Government puts forward to farmers across the nation. They are unacceptable. They will not deal with the distressing situation faced by farmers today. The Government should burn the midnight oil. The Minister should have a distressed look on his face because of the difficulties faced by farmers today and he is the Minister responsible in a national sense for that.
Hear, hear!
Are there any questions or comments relating to the Hon. Member's remarks? The Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse).

Mr. Speaker, I think the record should be corrected. The latter part of the speech of the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Scheilenberger) did not deal specifically with farm credit, but the Hon. Member became a little carried away with some of his interpretations of what had gone on in the Crow debate. Since it was allowed in the earlier part of his speech, Mr. Speaker, I hope you will permit me to make a short response.
The Hon. Member continues to misinterpret a very clear motion which we put forward concerning the rates that farm-

April 11, 1984
Supply
ers would pay under the Crow Bill. Our proposal was that the Crow rate was and should continue to be an average of $4.89 per tonne and that the safety net clause, which was extremely clear and which everyone understood except the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin and two or three of his confreres, included the provision that the percentage of freight to the price of grain could never go beyond a certain percentage.
What percentage?

I think at the moment it was 6 per cent. That would have provided protection when grain prices dropped. As grain prices dropped, that safety net would have had the effect, had the Hon. Member done the mathematics and understood the motion, of pulling the actual freight rate down from $1.89 on average per tonne instead of providing the tremendous increase which he interpreted. People outside the committee and people in the press understood it. Only a few Hon. Members in the House pretended not to be able to understand it.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member puts forward a pretty weak defence of his plan. If he had followed the leadership of my Party, he would have put forward a much simpler plan to freeze rates at the Crow level for farmers until the review process.
We have made the calculations very carefully. If his amendment had been in place, this year the safety net would not have been triggered until the $6 per tonne level had been reached. That is a little better than the Government's proposal which was $8 per tonne, but it certainly was not as good as ours. If our suggestion to freeze rate increases had been accepted, farmers would have been in tremendous shape this year and would not be facing increased freight costs when they cannot afford them.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) helped to make the point which the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) was making. The fact of the matter is that freight rate costs were equal to 2.5 per cent of the weighted average of grains sold. He said that they were asking for a safety net of 6 per cent, so it is very obvious that those who claimed to stand in defence of the Crow really, by the presentation of their amendment, contributed to the dismantlement of the Crow.
I would like to ask my colleague a question. I know that he and his family are engaged in a farming operation.
You cannot read, Don.
I can certainly understand your line of logic.
It was a frozen rate.

Mr. Speaker, he is stumbling over his own words. I cannot help it.
As I was saying, my colleague is engaged in a family farm operation. Could he explain to the House, on the basis of his
experience in his own operation, the impact of high interest rates, high input costs and low commodity prices, over which he as an individual manager-I hapen to know that he is a good manager because he keeps an accurate set of books-has no control?

Mr. Speaker, I hate to put this on the record. After farming for years, this year, as a result of interest rate costs, input costs and two years of relative drought in my area, we will have to cut the number of acres we seed in half just for the farming operation to stay alive. We have done everything according to the best research available. Even with two managing my family farm, we are incapable of continuing to farm the number of acres we have farmed in the past.
This is not unusual in our area. Almost all farmers in my region, given the situation and the climate in which they have been farming, are incapable of finding sufficient cash to put their crop in the ground this year. Ten per cent of them have been unable to pay the fuel bills for last year. The situation is serious. They are looking for an indication of some hope in the future, given reasonable weather conditions, that they will be able to continue to survive and to farm.
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, I have been listening carefully to the remarks made about the farming community by Members on the other side of the House. I am a little ill at ease to hear the many criticisms against the Government, especially that it is being unfair to farmers, who forever find themselves in a bad predicament. I am embarrassed for Canadian agricultural producers, and I think it must be said that their productivity is almost second to none. It is not true to say that Canada's farming community is in the doldrums and badly treated.
That is why I take this opportunity to tell the House about the many constructive measures the Government has been implementing for years on behalf of farmers, through the Farm Credit Corporation. Mr. Speaker, I cannot deny that the agricultural sector does experience serious difficulties, but the situation is not quite as desperate as some people would have us believe. The Canadian Government has given unfailing support to those Canadian farmers who have been hardest hit by the economic recession. This support is not just a fleeting trend since it dates back to 1929 when the Government established the Canadian Farm Loan Board to help farmers who were unable to secure the long-term credit they needed. The Board and its successor, the Farm Credit Corporation, have now been filling the void for 55 years. Just so Hon. Members will have an idea of the amount of money invested in agriculture by the Farm Credit Corporation, I point out that is has some 79,300 loans outstanding for a total investment of $4.7 billion right now.
April 11, 1984

Any way one looks at it, Mr. Speaker, that is a significant contribution to the economic well-being of Canadian farmers. During the year ended March 31, 1984, the Farm Credit Corporation authorized 5,736 loans under its regular credit program and the special agricultural financial assistance program, almost $758 million all told. That is $141 million more than the previous year. Mr. Speaker, it is a shame to claim that nothing is being done to meet the needs of Canadians farmers, and I wonder indeed what Hon. Members opposite would do.
Just recently, the Government approved a budget which increases to about $825 million the funds available through the Farm Credit Corporation for loans to Canada's farmers in 1984-85.
Pursuant to its terms of reference, the FCC helps young people and newcomers to farming, those whose equity falls short of the requirements of commercial lending institutions. The Farm Credit Corporation plays a key role. Neophyte farmers and owners of small farming operations in full expansion are much more vulnerable than long-time farmers. Since their assets are limited, they need quite a bit of capital to start and maintain profitable operations. That is why they must be able to borrow at preferential rates which commercial lenders cannot offer them.
