Mr. Speaker, I am sorry if I have misinterpreted what you said earlier, but I shall continue.
In the Canadian labour force, the only people genuinely able and willing to become farm producers are farmers' sons and daughters. They are the only ones who have the required knowledge and any practical experience in agriculture.
We must therefore encourage the transfer of farming operations to their generation if we want to keep these human resources in the field of agriculture and maintain or increase the productivity of the farming industry.
The only way this can happen is to offer these people reasonable interest rates and favourable credit terms, and this the commercial financial institutions do not normally do. In addition, a family farm is usually transferred on a step by step
Supply
basis. The son or the daughter generally buy the operation step by step while they obtain the funds and the experience required, and eventually take over the whole business. As the land itself is the basic requirement for most farm producers, newcomers usually need credit to purchase land. Farm real estate represents an average of nearly 80 per cent of total investment requirements in agriculture. Credit requirements for land purchases are therefore very high. Even though parents generally want to help a son or a daughter take over their farm, they must recover the accumulated assets in the farm if they want to be in a position to retire or divide their property equitably between all the members of their family. Even young farmers who are getting started with the help of their family will therefore need credit at conditions not generally offered by the commercial sector.
This is what the Farm Credit Corporation is offering them. At the present time, it is offering farm operators loans of a maximum of $350,000 or $600,000, depending on whether the operation includes one or more eligible applicants. The loan limits of the Farm Credit Corporation have been increased twice during the last three years to meet the needs of farmers more adequately.
In view of the special financing requirements of farm operations, the federal Government has offered them, through the Farm Credit Corporation, long term farm credit programs on terms which are not generally available neither to them nor to small businesses, so as to promote farm production. Such terms include mortgages at interest rates frozen for five, ten and twenty years, repayment periods of up to thirty years, flexible repayment schedules, a recovery policy which takes into account temporary financial difficulties and the cyclical nature of farm income, loans of up to 100 per cent of the assets stated as security, as well as a financial advice and consultation service for farmers.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that these new initiatives come at a time when producers need them the most, and I understand that these innovations were introduced by our Minister and the Farm Credit Corporation.
The FCC puts loads of energy into its consultation services program because farmers need to have a sound understanding of financial management in order to succeed. It provides counselling at the preliminary stage, when the loan is approved and at various stages afterwards. While financial counselling is available to all farmers, the Corporation takes special care of new borrowers or other borrowers in need or those who ask for assistance. Its counselling is aimed at helping farmers to run their financial operations and eventually achieve their personal and economic goals.
Borrowers from the Farm Credit Corporation who need counselling are generally those with small assets or large debts, with a developing operation, without experience, with a high-risk business or financial problems. The Corporation's credit counsellor provides borrowers with the assistance they need to

April 11, 1984
Supply
start a bookkeeping system, to interpret and analyze financial data, so that they can identify and solve problems as soon as they crop up.
Normally, borrowers also get involved in the program for two or three years. This is generally long enough for them to learn to manage their financial affairs efficiently. As of March 31, 1984, 4,800 FCC borrowers were involved in the consultation services program, which accounts for 30 per cent of all FCC borrowers.
In addition to offering this credit program, the FCC is co-operating with federal agencies and departments, provincial governments and private financial institutions in meeting the special needs of farmers. For several years, it has been co-operating with certain provinces, namely, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Alberta, by sharing the costs of their interest rate subsidization programs. The FCC intensified its efforts in this area in 1982-83 by participating in the Saskatchewan farm purchase program as a financing agency.
Fast year, the FCC also signed an agreement with the Province of Ontario to act as lender for the new farmers assistance program.
The FCC lends to farmers who represent high risks for the private sector. A survey carried out by the Corporation has indicated that the average Canadian farm had net assets of 85 per cent. On the other hand, those farmers who obtained a regular loan from the Canadian Farm Corporation had net assets of nearly 50 per cent during the last five years. The average net assets of farmers who obtained a loan under the special Farm Financial Assistance Program were even lower, namely 35 per cent during the 1983-84 fiscal year and 40 per cent the previous year.
The loan-to-equity ratio is also indicative of the risks taken. As the Farm Credit Corporation was authorized in 1975-76 to lend up to 100 per cent of the value of the property offered as equity the loan-to-security ratio is increasing. The Farm Credit Corporation has granted a greater proportion of its loans to farmers who offer less equity than in the past. This tendency to lend to farmers with lower net assets and a higher loan-to-equity ratio results from the fact that the Corporation is lending to younger farmers with limited resources and also from the difficult economic situation.
The special Farm Financial Assistance Program was reintroduced in the Budget of June 1982.
Foans to farmers under 35 continue to account for the larger part of the funds loaned by the Corporation making up 62 per cent of the total. Most of these farmers own little land and have few personal assets. Whether they want to get into farming or to extend their operations, these younger farmers must borrow large amounts for longer periods. Many of them, especially those who must consolidate their debts, cannot offer
additional equity, which means an even higher loan-to-equity ratio.
As Hon. Members are certainly aware, the Farm Credit Corporation has administered the special financial assistance program for agriculture ever since it was implemented in November 1981. Under this program, farmers facing financial disaster have access for two years to a rebate on their loans to the Farm Credit Corporation. Parliament has allocated funds to the Farm Credit Corporation to cover the rebate on these special loans. When the program was set up in November 1981, the Government had allocated to it a total of $50 million, including $5 million to cover the 5 per cent interest rebate which was its key-element. The funds so earmarked were spent very quickly, and the program expired on March 31, 1982. This time, the new program allowed for a 4 per cent interest rebate. Moreover, a budget of $200 million was allocated to this program, with some $16 million earmarked for interest rebates. This program was extended again in the April 1983 budget. Then the Government came up with an additional $100 million. Between November 1981 and March 31, 1984, the Farm Credit Corporation has spent over $341.1 million on this program, and over 2,200 Canadian farmers have received or are still receiving benefits under this program. When the Government implemented this program, it expected an economic recovery within the next two years during which the rebate program would apply. We are aware that the recovery in agriculture has been slow. The Government is currently looking into a possible extension of the rebate period and other means to help farmers in financial distress. As the minister has indicated, a decision is forthcoming.
I should emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that the role of the Farm Credit Corporation is not to provide mortgage loans to all farmers, but only to high risk ones. The Farm Credit Corporation has not been established to discharge banks from their responsibilities or to provide credit to commercial farms. At the end of the seventies, at a time when the agricultural economy was at its best, commercial lenders asked for a larger share of that market. In spite of a slowdown in the farming sector, I expect that they will continue to lend to farmers.
The Government follows very closely the trend of the longterm farm credit market. It is looking into various options which would allow it to provide funds to the Farm Credit Corporation. The latter, on the other hand, is now considering the means of lowering the rates on those high-interest loans. The Government's commitment to agriculture is unequivocal and we are trying our best to give a new impetus to the industry while it is still emerging from the recession. I would like to remind Hon. Members that the Farm Credit Corporation is one of the few lending institutions to have a repayment policy based on the cyclical nature of farm revenues. As long as any undertaking stands a fair chance of pulling itself out of a precarious financial situation, the FCC will be there to help. The federal Government supports the agricultural sector
April 11, 1984

through credit programs to help farmers maintain prosperous operations. Through the Farm Credit Corporation's long- and medium-term mortgage loan programs guaranteed under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the federal Government makes sure that Canada's agriculture ranks among the most efficient and most productive sectors of the Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, that is the message I wanted to convey today on behalf of the Canadian Government and the Farm Credit Corporation in answer to Hon. Members who keep saying that nothing has been done for the farming community. The truth is that the Farm Credit Corporation may just be the organization which on many occasions in the past two years has been prepared to come to the rescue of financially threatened agricultural operations. Mr. Speaker, that is why many laws were passed to help the most needy through every kind of low-interest program which kept those farmers active and productive.
More legislation is forthcoming to help farmers who are still experiencing hardship. I might say again that the Government and the private sector ought to share this role to support the farming community, particularly when it is going through hard times.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions or comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to join in this debate today to share the concerns of many of my colleagues about what we are debating today and to talk about the insensitivity and disregard of the Government for the agricultural sector of the country. This is not a very nice subject to have to talk about. The fact that we must remind the Government of its responsibility to an industry which overall employs about 18 per cent of the labour force, represents about 40 per cent of Canada's economy, accounts for 10 per cent of our exports, and generates $7 for every SI spent, is, simply put, appalling.
While the Government appears to be willing to provide money, incentives such as rebates, tax credits and so on in large amounts to so many other sectors, it is completely unwilling to respond in a positive way to the demands of agriculture. When a positive step is taken, it is generally only as a result of years of complaint from the farmers themselves and from this side of the House. The Government appears to be unwilling to take the initiative to place agriculture high enough on its list of priorities. This is the root of the problem.
The biggest crisis is the unavailability of affordable credit. Interest rates now appear to be on the rise again; we are seeing that every day. We have just come out of a period of very high interest rates. They were as high as 21.24 per cent in August of 1981 and even higher for some first mortgages. According to the Conference Board of Canada, continuing high levels of interest rates are going to be one of the major factors in a projected slow down in the economy. This is occurring at a
Supply
time when farmers can least afford an increase in the rates of credit. Unlike other sectors, agriculture is still hurting from the recent recession. Last year farm bankruptcies were up 16 per cent from 1982; they rose from 410 to 488. Ontario let the nation with a total of 165 declared bankruptcies. There were probably as many or even more, undeclared bankruptcies. Prairie farm failures doubled last year. By the end of February this year farm bankruptcies were up 58 per cent over the same period last year.
The main point that must be made, Mr. Speaker, is that farmers are still hurting very badly. They have not seen this recovery of which the Liberals boast. A very well respected financial constultant was quoted recently in the London Free Press as saying that many farmers continue to suffer the painful hangover of recession. Some may never get over it. If interest rates rise now many will be forced into the red and off the farm. He estimates about 40 per cent of farmers are in financial difficulty. If banks and governments keep hiding their heads in the sand, no solution is possible for farmers.
The outlook for farmers is not good, Mr. Speaker. Debt loads carried by agriculture will soon reach $20 billion. Farm input costs are high and have increased at a much higher rate than prices which farmers receive for their products. Many inputs which farmers have to buy are paid for on credit in anticipation of future harvests. With high levels of credit, high costs become almost unbearable. In most cases they become so unbearable that a farmer is forced into bankruptcy or into selling the farm at a reduced price.
Let us look for a minute at the cost of interest rates on the purchase of a used tractor. You cannot buy much of a tractor for $25,000. Anyone who knows anything about agriculture knows that is a very small tractor. Very often we are faced with prices of tractors anywhere from $45,000, $55,000 or $60,000 to $90,000 or $100,000. Many farmers require that size of a tractor, but we will use a $25,000 tractor as an example.
A $25,000 tractor purchased on a five-year credit would cost $31,860 in total at 10 per cent interest. At 15 per cent interest it would cost $35,700. At 20 per cent that $25,000 tractor would cost almost $40,000. I am not saying for a moment that farmers are the only ones who have this sort of problem. I am saying that farmers are often ignored in this country, especially by the Government which does not seem to realize the enormous costs which go into maintaining a farm to produce food for Canadians and for export.
At this point in time, after the cumulative effects of recession, inflation and high interest rates, as well as low commodity prices, there are 14,000 Farm Credit Corporation loans in arrears, or 18 per cent of all Farm Credit Corporation loans. I am saying that farmers already face a serious situation and they cannot afford higher interest rates and further insensitivity by the Government to their situation.
So what happens? Over the past few weeks we have watched as the Government continues to neglect the agricultural sector. Instead of responding to the situation and trying to implement serious policies which can take some of the burden off

like so many things before it. They will die in the same way Bill C-653, the Farm Creditors Arrangement Act, died and we will have to bring the matter up again. In the meantime, the legislation could be passed if a sub-committee was created. But again the Government has indicated its lack of interest in the agricultural sector.
We have seen so often in the past that a low priority is placed on agriculture by this Government and we are right now watching history repeat itself. Hon. Members opposite do not care about agriculture any more now than they have in past decades.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, we in this Party are often accused of having no policy. Well, we are discussing our policy today. The Government is well aware of our policy because we have been discussing these and other issues for many years. The problem is that the Government will not listen to our policies and implement them to the benefit not only of farmers but of the Canadian consumer who buys the products of farmers' labour. This is why we are cynical about the Government, especially with regard to agriculture. We have been driven to a strong sense of cynicism about what the future brings as a direct result of our observation of the way in which this Government abandons its responsibilities, particularly with regards to farmers.
We have alternatives, Mr. Speaker, simply because we care. We have not forgotten that it was farmers who built this country and made it strong. We know that things can be better for farmers with a series of measures, most importantly the maintenance of affordable credit for farmers. In part, this means that the Government must take responsibility for the economy in order to keep interest rates in general at affordable rates. We are not sure that the Government can do that either. It must, Mr. Speaker, look carefully at these issues, and more importantly at its own priorities, because farmers cannot bear a repeat of the last few years so soon. If farmers are in trouble, we are all in very serious trouble.
I have always maintained-I am sure many of my colleagues will agree-that if we have a strong agricultural base, we will have a very viable country. We know that farmers are great spenders. If they receive even an expectation of a good crop and a reasonable price, they will usually purchase machinery and in so doing stimulate the economy. I say everything starts with the soil in this country. If we can give some direction and offer of hope to these farmers who are producing the fine food, not only for us but for people in many parts of the world, I think we have a duty and obligation to do so in order to ensure we have a strong and viable agriculture industry.

Mr. Speaker, I believe a lot of what the Hon. Member for Huron-Bruce (Mr. Cardiff) has said is basic to this country. I particularly agree with his strong statement that if we have a healthy agricultural sector in Canada we have the makings of a very strong base for our entire economy. I just wanted to stand up and tell him that I believe what he
Supply
said is excellent and should be repeated. I also want to say that he is a person who has a great deal of credibility because of the work he has done in this House and on behalf of his constituents.
I certainly do not agree with all the Hon. Member's rhetoric to the extent that Liberal Members on this side do not care about farmers. However, if we can get away from political partisanship here, I believe that working constructively together we have to follow his line, which is to ensure that the farmers in this country do have a strong economic base for carrying on their activities. We look forward to continuing the constructive dialogue on the positive ways in which these types of things can be achieved.
I would also like to say that I know the Hon. Member is aware of the fact that it is really not true that the Government has done nothing for the farmers in this country. I am sure he will admit that. Even in his area, for example, CIDA, the Canadian International Development Agency, purchases an incredible number of edible beans for shipment to Third World countries. We have a foreign aid package which is among the best in the world in terms of food aid and which does directly help the farmers.
I have one question for the Hon. Member. He referred in the opening of his speech to a newspaper called the London Free Press. Is that the scurrilous Tory rag which is owned by Peter White?
You are like the cow that kicked the pail of milk over, are you not?

Mr. Speaker, I have no idea who owns the London Free Press. However, I thank the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) for his comments. I do not know if it is appropriate to ask him to be my campaign manager in the upcoming election or not!
He will not have anything else to do!

Well, I do not know. That could be a possibility.
The Hon. Member touched on many subjects, such as CIDA and foreign aid, and I believe we must congratulate our farmers in this country for producing this food. And yes, I do support the positions taken in the purchase of food, and not only white beans, because as the Hon. Member knows full well, there are many other commodities across this country which the food aid program purchases and sends to countries in distress or in need. As the Hon. Member said, if we work together we can do many of these things. I am sure that if there was an offer of co-operation, he would find a lot more co-operation coming from this side, such as on the agri-bond issue. That is an issue we would have liked to deal with very quickly. Perhaps the Hon. Member could encourage some of his colleagues to help us get that matter back to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs much faster.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should point out to my colleague across the floor that the previous Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance moved in this House on February 7 that the agri-bond issue be sent to the Finance Committee for study. I seconded the motion. The fact remains that the other items before the committee dragged on to the point where we I had a first meeting on this last Thursday. However, I am somewhat disappointed in that we had to ask the researcher from the Finance Committee to bring forward a background paper on this issue because there are several variations which were put forward, generally that lenders would obtain a tax benefit for interest on eligible funds loaned. It was also suggested that the tax benefit be restructured as a credit rather than an exemption to improve the fairness of the measure. And, of course, this applies to eligible funds that we have loaned to farmers at presumably lower than market rates.
There are other areas which I know Hon. Members of Parliament, and particularly members of the Finance Committee, will want to look at in depth. The reason is that this is a tax measure which is important to the future financing of the agricultural industry. But no lending program is going to cure all the problems of the industry in Canada.
When we look at farm cash receipts of a few years ago, as well as the total investment, they increased from $24 billion in 1971 to $132 billion in 1982; a tremendous increase. During the same period production costs have increased sharply from $2.9 billion in 1971 to $12.8 billion in 1982. They are up again this year. Total farm credit increased from $2.2 billion in 1970 to $10.3 billion in 1981, dropping slightly in 1982. With greater amounts of credit being extended each year, total farm debt increased from $4.4 billion in 1970 to $20.2 billion in 1982. The debt-equity ratio in 1972 compared to 1982 deteriorated slightly and I expect it will deteriorate further as we get the figures in for 1983 and 1984. In 1983 total cash receipts amounted to $18.8 billion, and expenses to $15.5 billion, leaving a net income of about $3.6 billion. In 1984, realized net farm income is expected to increase to $3.9 billion, or about 6 per cent.
Today the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellen-berger) stated that farmers are price takers, not price setters. I want to remind the Opposition that we have marketing legislation in Canada which will allow farm groups to organize so that they can set their own prices. This is available at both federal and provincial government levels. Those producers who have chosen to use this legislation have been able to pass on their increased costs and ride out the variables of input costs much better than those who have not taken advantage of it.
If we are to look at farming as a business, then we must have a counterbalance in the system to enable our farmers to obtain a reasonable return on their investment; a return for management and risk, a return which will allow them to live a
life commensurate with that of the rest of society. They can take advantage of the provisions of the Budget of February 15 which will allow them to invest in RRSPs. They can defer the payment of capital gains tax.
Let us look at that in its total context. If a man had an operation that was worth $120,000 when capital gains tax first came in, and it increased to $360,000 in 1984, he would have a capital gain of $240,000, half of which is taxable. He could invest the other $120,000 in RRSPs. This has been a tremendous step forward for Canadian farmers and has been well accepted, certainly by the Canadian federation of Agriculture and other commodity groups.
I quite realize that opposition members today have not said much about improving cash flow in the farming sector and changing the position of farmers from that of price takers to that of price setters. Can they explain just what the price determination factor is in the futures market? Is it based on rumours which can set off speculative trading? Does it sometimes reflect the buying power of a few large multinational grain companies? This exemplifies the need for a countervailing force in the system. Canadian farmers have legislation which enables them to receive a domestic price for wheat and an export price. I fully realize that with the prices of the last few years the difference has not been significant, but the precedent has been set.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has reached an agreement with four of his provincial counterparts to proceed with the tripartite stabilization program to provide a measure of relief to some of our producers. But I maintain that we cannot stop there. We have to continue to seek out better mechanisms to ensure that the cash flow of our farmers is such that they can pay off their borrowings. They cannot borrow their way out of trouble. There has to be a cash flow and a system which ensures a return so they can expand their operation and take advantage of our position in export markets.
Look at what is happening in the European Common Market with their accumulated surpluses. We should encourage our producers to re-examine legislation at provincial and federal levels to ensure the cash flow of the efficient Canadian producer is maintained. The Minister is presently in his office meeting with the Deputy Minister of Agriculture from Thailand. They are seeking opportunities through Canadian technology to enhance their own operations. But I think Canadian farmers have a tremendous opportunity available to them.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) today asked a question regarding the tax on farm fuels. He gave a figure of about $250 million as the saving to farmers. This amounts to 1 per cent of farm input costs for 1983. Therefore, no one program will resolve the financial hardships we have in the Canadian agricultural industry at the present time. I maintain that we have to look at a series of programs which will not only provide for long-term stability, but also a series of programs which will allow them an adequate return on their investment, management and risk.
April 11, 1984

Mr. Speaker, the figures that have been tossed around this afternoon have sort of made one wonder what is the relative position of the farmer with respect to income on his equity invested. The Federation of Agriculture has provided us with some figures today. I would like to point out that in 1982 the net income of farmers was $3,696 billion. That net income arose from an equity position of the farmers of $111,853 billion. If you relate the net income of the farmer to his equity, you find that the farmer has made about 3.5 per cent on his equity.
If, on the other hand, you relate the farmer to any other form of business, you find the farmer on average has a very high percentage of his investment, relatively speaking, in land which is not depreciable. If the equity position of the farmer were totally depreciable, as many businesses are nearly totally depreciable, there would not be a net income for the farming community at all.
I think it is interesting to note also from these figures that from 1971 to 1984 there was an increment of income for the farmer in real dollars of $76 million. But there were 316,770 farmers which means the real increase in income of the farmer in that 14-year period was 250 real dollars per farmer.
When any Minister of the Crown can stand in this House and say that he has done well by agriculture, as he presided as Minister in 13 of those 14 years, I wonder what he would consider is a bad job. What would be a bad job in his estimation? I would like to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that from 1971 to 1982 the indebtedness of farmers went up, according to my hasty calculations, something over 700 per cent. That is so the farmer can make an increment of income of 250 real dollars. If we carry that a little further, we find the interest load is up 700 per cent. If you go a little further, you will find that the net realized income for a self-employed farmer for man-years, not counting the free labour of the family on the farm, has increased by 25 per cent. The farmer has had a 25 per cent increase, with free labour, in net income but he has had a 700 per cent increase in interest and he has had maybe a 750 per cent increase in his indebtedness.
I want to tell you, Sir, that when you get an increment in terms of 700 per cent versus 3.5 per cent you are not very solid and your industry is in very very shaky shape. I want to tell you also that in the general structure of regulated industries, such as the public utilities of Canada, you are allowed something in the nature of 15 per cent return on your equity. You are also allowed, if you are an operator of a public utility, an increment on an annual basis which will approach that return of 15 per cent on your equity, and the farmer is getting 3.5 per cent.
Maybe farmers are as prosperous and as well off as the Minister stated they were today, but they are not as well off as the public utilities by any stretch of the imagination, and they are totally regulated by the governments of this land. If, and I want to emphasize this, the farmer could depreciate as much
Supply
of his percentage of property which he has invested as Canada public utilities, it would be an interesting economic problem to study and I think you would find that he would then show a net loss. That is not very good.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that you are as interested as I am in the health of certain aspects of the agricultural industry, particularly potatoes. I want to ask the Minister why he has not at this time addressed the application of the Province of New Brunswick for price stabilization for the 1982-83 crop year. There was a point in time when there was reason for delay in consideration of that application. That reason has now gone by. The farmers have now planted a second crop since that crop was harvested and it is high time that that application for price stabilization is given favourable consideration by the Government in the generous terms which the industry requires and which you and I both, I am sure, Sir, want to see for our farmers. The application has been on the desk for quite some time and it has not been considered.
During the remarks of the Minister today he suggested that certain areas of agriculture should organize. I am going to ask him to address the same problem that I have asked him to address every time he has thrown that piece of slop across the floor. When he gets a task force to investigate the possibilities of supply management and price control in a product which is so variable in its annual yield that we have shortages and surpluses, perhaps he could get that task force to address also the vital necessity of international trade, whether it be maple syrup, white beans, apples, potatoes, carrots and onions. International trade is a vital part of the production of virtually all of the fruits and vegetables of the Dominion of Canada and if we can address the means by which we can retain our international markets, while at the same time introducing supply and price management, then I would be very happy.
This is a problem that has been addressed by agricultural organizations but they have not come up with the answer. I want it to be addressed in such a way that we do not upset our trade patterns. The Government on the one hand is preaching free trade for Canada in the world, but on the other hand it is asking for supply management and price controls on fruits and vegetables-if we are going to get price stabilization for any of those products anywhere in Canada.
This does not make sense, Mr. Speaker. By doing that we are breaking the GATT rules and regulations to which we have subscribed. We will be putting up trade barriers on other items because, in retribution for our violation of our agreement, they will certainly seek a price. It is not a simple thing. We did close our doors to international trade, except by permit in the poultry and egg industry. That did not make us any friends. We have closed the doors in the dairy industry. In these instances we have got away with supply management and price control. But if we expand this, the international price in trade will be more than Canada can bear. We have to realize that and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has to realize it.
I do not like to be scorned by the Minister, Mr. Speaker. I do not like my people to be scorned by him either. But that is

precisely what he is doing. Because there is no supply management, he says we should not get price stabilization, although the Act entitled fruit and vegetable growers-organised or unorganised, it does not specify-to an element of assistance which approaches cost of production on a near automatic basis. That is what we have been denied.
I challenge the Minister as he was earlier challenged, I believe by the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellen-berger), on the basis of how can we on the one hand criticize the United States for constraining production and on the other hand proffer the idea that there should be supply management and price control in any agricultural product? It sort of looks to me as though we are standing in a glass house hurling stones, which is not a very good process to follow. The input costs have not become the proper factor to establish a base price for any assistance which would be given. This has been proven in western stabilization and in the approach of the Department of Agriculture to the fruit and vegetable side of our farm business. For instance, the fact that some costs such as interest rates have gone up as much as 700 per cent has not been taken into account, and whatever yearly average price the Minister may take does not necessarily approach the stock loss requirements that price stabilization has historically provided.
However, I hope that the Minister will soon address this problem and on behalf of the farmers of my constituency I hope he will address the removal of some of the tax on farm fuels. It involves a huge amount of money in our constituencies and it is a problem that must be addressed.
We must redefine what a farmer is for tax purposes. For example, a farmer may have had the misfortune to have a five-year loss. He might have to seek extra income to stay on his farm and retain his investment. There is no way that someone who has probably never turned a furrow in his life and has no conception of the inner thoughts of a man who is trying to farm should be able to assess and tax him as a part-time or hobby farmer. These cases must be assessed on individual facts and cannot be covered by blanket guidelines or the judgment of one person.
I see that Members from both sides of the House are in fact interested in agriculture. We must address this issue in a unified fashion in order to alleviate the difficulties in which our farmers presently find themselves. Indeed, they should be treated like small businessmen. When a small businessman takes outside employment it does not affect his income. He is taxed on his total net income and his business is not anticipated as being non-profit. The accumulation of his income is taxable, as it should be with so many of our farmers.
I could name a farmer in your constituency, Mr. Speaker, who certainly needs that kind of attention because he has been taxed unmercifully as a result of unknowledgeable people assessing him for what they thought he was rather than what he did in the community.
This is not a political question; it is a matter of discussing right and wrong, fairness and equity. This issue needs the
support of the people to your right, Mr, Speaker, as well as the pleas from people to your left.
Today the Minister said that the tripartite principle of red meat programs was totally accepted by the producers. I talked to a producer from New Brunswick who does not accept the principle of the proposed formula as he understood it. In Atlantic Canada we are paying $50 per tonne more for corn or western barley or wheat. He tells me that if a farmer in our area must pay that much more for his grain than a farmer in another area of Canada, and if Atlantic Canada is to retain any segment of the red meat industry, then that program must be formulated in such a way that it will trigger a payment at a particular percentage of cost in a particular province or region. Until that problem is addressed, Atlantic Canada red meat producers are very concerned that they may be left out in the cold. They are not ready to support any tripartite Bill which may come to the House of Commons.
The Minister is absent while this subject matter is being discussed. I submit that that is disrespectful. While I accept the fact that all Members of Parliament have responsibilities, in view of the Minister's bragging I think he should at least be able to brag that he is in the House on days when subject matters concerning his ministry are discussed. He is not here today and I do not believe he was here when this subject was discussed previously. He should be here in view of the magnitude of interest in this subject that has been shown by farmers.
When the Minister introduces more legislation on any subject matter, I ask him to consider the representations made by the farmers of Canada on a regional basis, as they must be if the program is to be universally accepted. There is great room for improvement. A 3.5 per cent return on equity for a farmer with only a fraction of his investment being depreciable is not good enough. A 15 per cent return, such as it is for a public utility, is more likely to provide the profit which is needed. That is government approved. Let us address this as a real problem and not play games or brag any more. Let us produce.

speechtext: Are there questions or comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, when the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) said that he was going to share an exciting new development with us, my friend from Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) was hoping that he was going to announce to the House that the research centre he was speaking of had developed a tree that grows money! I am sure many farmers would find something like that very attractive.
It is better than that. You can't eat money.

With respect to the motion and the concerns of the Farm Credit Corporation, I received a phone call yesterday morning from one of my constituents who just heard the happy news that the Farm Credit Corporation had increased its interest rates again from 13 per cent to 14 per cent, 14 and %ths per cent and 15 per cent. Of course, I say he was happy somewhat facetiously. He was not happy at all. Indeed, toward the end of our brief conversation he was asking what he had to do to make the Government notice the fact that farmers could not afford any more increases in their interest rates at this time.
He concluded by asking if it is necessary for him to drive his tractor from Manitoba to Ottawa and then do something with it that I cannot say in the House since it would be unparliamentary. But it is an example of how frustrated many farmers have become with the increasing costs of operating a farm, the decreasing returns and the increasing difficulties they are facing in trying to simply stay alive.
I am fairly familiar with this person who phoned me. He is a good farmer who has quite good land and modern equipment. He has quite a bit of land. He is a good manager but he still has troubles in that there is so much stacked against him with all the increased costs.
In the past few months we have seen the changes in the Crow rate. Just by a fluke more than anything else, the area in which he lives was one of the latter blocks to be opened up for Wheat Board quotas, so his cash flow has been delayed. Also by a fluke of nature, in the last few years there have been problems with the weather. One year there was an early frost, another year there was too much rain and last summer there was serious drought. For those of us who are non-farmers, last year it was a beautiful summer in Manitoba. It was hot and dry. It was great for outdoor activities such as going to the beaches.
I thought you did not have any beaches out there.

We have beautiful beaches in Manitoba, Howard. For most farmers in Manitoba, last year's weather
Supply
was not at all good. I have talked with farmers in my home town and with farmers throughout my constituency who have told me about kernels of grain actually cooking in the head as they stood in the fields because of extreme temperatures.
Approximately six weeks ago when Parliament recessed, I spent all that time travelling around my constituency and holding public meetings with anyone who wanted to attend. At every one of the meetings there were at least one or two, a half dozen or in some cases quite a few farmers who came to discuss their general concerns. We also spent some time talking about their specific concerns. It was a bit of a lesson for me. We discussed things about which I heard a bit but I certainly had room to learn more. Some of their problems- and that is what a farmer who telephoned me told me yesterday-related to the cost of their loans and the increasing cost of fuels. In every community which I visited I was asked why the tax on farm fuels could not be reduced. I must admit that I agree with them on that. It would be very good for any government to give farmers a little break, at least in the cost of their fuels. Fuel costs have increased incredibly in recent years. It is a matter which we must address very soon. Coupled with these increased costs is the fact that their returns or the prices they are receiving for their products have either remained the same or in many cases have fallen in recent years.
In one such community, the Town of Riverton, there were some unique problems. For seven of the last eight years-I spoke about this matter in another debate in the House a few weeks ago, but certainly it is worth repeating because it highlights one critical situation in my constituency-farmers in the Riverton area have experienced crop failure. In normal times this is a fairly good farming area. They have good land and normally had good weather conditions until eight years ago. For some strange reason, in seven of the last eight years they have been hit by serious drought, then serious flooding and crop failures. Most businesses which have had failure for seven years out of eight would be lucky still to be in existence. However, these farmers have struggled. They have found money, they have scraped it together and have pulled in their belts a little tighter. They have mortgaged some of their property, but it is reaching a point where it is almost too much. They have gone to the banks and to credit unions in their community. They have gone to the Farm Credit Corporation looking for more money just to put in this year's crop. The ones who visited me-and there were a number of them-did not lead me to believe that it involved just a few farmers who were perhaps bad managers. I was told that probably 50 per cent of the farmers in the general area of Riverton were living under similar conditions.
A new crop season is starting any day now. Last weekend I spoke with a few farmers in my constituency who told me that with the very mild and dry spring in Manitoba this year they could be out in their fields as soon as next weekend. However, the farmers in Riverton may not be able to go into their fields because they do not have any money with which to put in this year's crop. They do not have any money to buy fuel, seed or fertilizer. What can they do? FCC will not give it to them nor

April 11, 1984
Supply
any of the other lending agencies. They are leery to give them any more money because there is no guarantee that this year will be a good one for crops.
Last Friday night I talked to a gentleman who is somewhat renowned in Manitoba. His name is Anton Chorney and he is from East Selkirk. He is a weather prognosticator and he told me that his prediction for 1984 is another hot and dry summer like last year for Manitoba. Certainly that is not good news for any farmer in the province.
What do I tell these farmers who have experienced so many crop failures? They do not have any guarantee that this year will not be the same as seven of the last eight years. They are carrying large debt loads. They have been farmers all their lives. It is not easy for them to change occupations. Even at the best of times when there are lots of jobs in other sectors of the economy, it is not easy for farmers to change their way of life, let alone at times such as this with high unemployment rates. What do I tell them that their Government in Ottawa is doing for them? What do I tell them that the FCC is prepared to do for them?
About a month ago I spoke in the House about farm issues. I said at that time that the Government had to make a decision as to whether or not it wanted family farms to continue to exist. I grew up on the Prairies. I am not a farm boy. I had very little to do with farms other than visiting some in my community from time to time. However, I learned from growing up on the Prairies about the sanctity of the family farm, that the family farm was the basis of prairie life.
Not only are farmers faced with the costs about which I have spoken but they have been subjected to the despicable way in which Revenue Canada has picked on them in recent months. This matter has been highlighted by both Parties on this side of the House. The Government seems to be following
policies which are not in favour of the continued existence of family farms. I am working on a case involving a couple of young brothers in my constituency who have taken over their father's farm. They are in their late twenties and are in serious trouble for the same reasons-crop failure in 1980, not a very good crop in 1981. They had to mortgage their house and then some of their property to keep the farm going. This farm has been in their family for 50 years as of this year. The FCC sent them a notice through its lawyer in Winnipeg on March 10 this year indicating that if they did not come up with $50,000-I cannot quite remember the figure-within 20 days, their farm would be taken away. How can they find this amount of money at the beginning of the crop year? They told me that if they use the money which they might have to put in this year's crop to pay FCC by April 1, they would be unable to plant and that would certainly scuttle their farm. They promised FCC that if it waited until the fall they would be able to make the payments. The matter is still being considered at this time by FCC. I have written to the Minister about this situation. I hope he will look at what is going on with these two young men who are starting out in life. They closed one of their letters by saying that they were disillusioned and disheartened. I do not think that is the kind of Canada we want.
I see that it is the end of the day. I thank the House for the opportunity to say a few words on this important motion.
